title: one-to-one correspondence and many-to-one correspondence, using double bar graphs

lesson.title: One Square Can Stand for a Whole Group!

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! At snack time our class counted fruit: four apples, six bananas, and three oranges. We drew a graph where every little square meant exactly one piece of fruit. Four squares for apples, six for bananas, three for oranges. We call that one-to-one correspondence, because one square matches one real thing.

visual.caption: One-to-one: one square means one piece of fruit

steps.say: But then our school ran a recycling drive, and our class collected one hundred forty cans! Imagine drawing one hundred forty tiny squares. Your hand would fall off! So we made a smarter rule: let one square stand for ten cans. Now thirty cans is only three squares, because thirty is three groups of ten. When one symbol stands for a whole group, we call it many-to-one correspondence.

visual.caption: Three squares, each square a group of ten cans

steps.say: Let's practise making the squares. Our bake sale sold twenty cookies on Monday, thirty-five on Tuesday, and fifteen on Wednesday. This time one square stands for five cookies. To find how many squares to draw, we divide. Twenty divided by five is four squares. Thirty-five divided by five is seven squares. Fifteen divided by five is three squares.

visual.caption: Real amount on top, squares to draw below

steps.say: Now let's read a graph backwards, which is what a real chart asks you to do. Tuesday's bar is seven squares tall. Seven squares, and each one is worth five cookies, so seven times five equals thirty-five cookies. The little note that says one square equals five cookies is called the key, and it is the most important part of the whole graph.

visual.caption: Key: one square = 5 cookies, so 7 squares = 35

steps.say: Here comes the fun part, a double bar graph. Two divisions in our school raced to collect cans for four days, so each day gets two bars standing side by side, one for Division A and one for Division B. Our key says one square equals ten cans. On Monday, Division A's bar is three squares, so three times ten is thirty cans. Division B's bar is two squares, so two times ten is twenty cans.

visual.caption: Double bar graph, key: one square = 10 cans

steps.say: Let's answer two real questions from that graph. On Wednesday, Division A got forty cans and Division B got sixty cans, so Division B collected sixty take away forty, which is twenty more cans. Now the totals. Division A: thirty plus fifty is eighty, plus forty is one hundred twenty, plus twenty is one hundred forty cans. Division B: twenty plus forty is sixty, plus sixty is one hundred twenty, plus fifty is one hundred seventy cans. So Division B won by one hundred seventy take away one hundred forty, which is thirty cans.

visual.caption: Division B collected 30 more cans in total

steps.say: One last warning from Ms. Yuanyuan. If a bar is six squares tall and the key says one square equals ten, the answer is not six! It is six times ten, which is sixty. So every single time you look at a graph, read the key first, then multiply. That one habit will keep your answers correct.

lesson.answer: One-to-one means one square equals one thing; many-to-one means one square stands for a group, so read the key first and multiply.

practice.question: At a Victoria school bottle drive, a double bar graph has this key: one square stands for 20 bottles. Division 1's bar is 5 squares tall and Division 2's bar is 8 squares tall. How many bottles did each division collect, and how many more did Division 2 collect?
practice.answer: Division 1: 5 x 20 = 100 bottles. Division 2: 8 x 20 = 160 bottles. Division 2 collected 160 - 100 = 60 more bottles.
